guide.summary: Unit 1 covers how ecosystems are structured and how matter and energy move through them: species interactions, terrestrial and aquatic biomes, the carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water cycles, primary productivity, and energy flow through trophic levels. Expect calculations with the 10% rule and productivity, and questions on which reservoirs and processes dominate each cycle.

sections.heading: Species interactions and biomes
sections.body: Predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism shape communities. Competition can lead to resource partitioning: species divide a resource by time (temporal), location (spatial), or form (morphological). Biomes are defined by average temperature and precipitation, which set the dominant plants. Tundra: cold, permafrost, short growing season. Boreal forest (taiga): cold, conifers, nutrient-poor acidic soils. Temperate deciduous forest: four seasons, fertile soil. Grassland and savanna: seasonal rain, fire, grazing; savannas are warm with a long dry season. Desert: under ~25 cm of precipitation per year. Tropical rainforest: warm, wet year-round, very high productivity but thin nutrient-poor soils because nutrients are locked in biomass. Aquatic biomes are set by salinity, depth, flow, and temperature; estuaries, salt marshes, and mangroves are highly productive because rivers and tides deliver nutrients.

sections.heading: Biogeochemical cycles
sections.body: Carbon: the largest reservoirs are sedimentary rock and the deep ocean (long-term); fast exchanges are photosynthesis and respiration between atmosphere and biosphere. Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from a long-term reservoir to the atmosphere faster than it returns. Nitrogen: the atmosphere (N₂) is the largest reservoir but unusable by most organisms; nitrogen fixation (bacteria, lightning, Haber–Bosch) makes NH₃/NH₄⁺, nitrification makes NO₂⁻ and NO₃⁻, assimilation incorporates nitrogen into organisms, ammonification returns it to soil, and denitrification (anaerobic bacteria) returns N₂ to the air. Phosphorus: no significant atmospheric phase; it moves from rock by weathering, so it is slow and often the limiting nutrient in freshwater. Water: evaporation and transpiration (together evapotranspiration) driven by solar energy; oceans are the largest reservoir, and most fresh water is in ice caps and groundwater.

sections.heading: Productivity and energy flow
sections.body: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate of photosynthesis; net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP − respiration by producers, the energy available to consumers. In aquatic systems, productivity is often measured with light and dark bottles: the light bottle's oxygen change is NPP, the dark bottle's loss is respiration, and GPP = NPP + respiration. Productivity is highest where sunlight, water, warmth, and nutrients are abundant. Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost mostly as heat from metabolism (second law of thermodynamics). This limits food chains to a few levels and makes top predators sensitive to disruption.

sections.heading: Worked example: energy flow
sections.body: If producers in an ecosystem capture 20,000 kcal/m²/yr, the 10% rule predicts about 2,000 kcal available to primary consumers, 200 to secondary consumers, and 20 to tertiary consumers. The rest is lost mainly as heat through cellular respiration. This explains why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels and why eating lower on the food chain can feed more people. Net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus the energy producers use for respiration; if GPP is 3,000 and respiration is 1,200, NPP is 1,800 kcal/m²/yr.

sections.heading: Cycles on the exam
sections.body: Questions frequently ask how human activities disrupt biogeochemical cycles. Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from long-term reservoirs (sediments, fossil fuels) to the atmosphere. Fertilizer runoff adds nitrogen and phosphorus to waterways, causing eutrophication. The phosphorus cycle has no significant atmospheric component, so phosphorus is often a limiting nutrient. Nitrogen fixation converts N₂ into ammonia, usable by plants; denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse gross and net productivity, forget that energy flows while matter cycles, and mix up nitrification and denitrification.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know biome, producer, consumer, decomposer, trophic level, food web, GPP, NPP, 10% rule, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and hydrologic cycles, and symbiosis types.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Free-response questions often present a food web or energy pyramid and ask you to calculate energy transfer, explain the effect of removing a species, or describe how a human activity alters a nutrient cycle. Identify the specific mechanism, such as fertilizer runoff increasing nitrogen in a lake, and connect it to an ecological effect.

keyTakeaways: 10% rule: each level up keeps about one-tenth of the energy.
Phosphorus has no atmospheric phase and is often limiting.
Denitrification returns N₂ to the atmosphere in anaerobic conditions.
Fossil fuel combustion moves carbon from long-term to short-term reservoirs.
Biomes are set by temperature and precipitation.
commonMistakes: Saying energy is recycled in ecosystems (matter cycles; energy flows and is lost as heat).
Using the dark bottle change as GPP.
Forgetting that transpiration is part of the water cycle.
examTips: Expect a 10% rule calculation and a productivity calculation.
Cycle questions often ask which process or reservoir; name it precisely.
Climatographs (temperature + precipitation by month) identify biomes; check the dry season.
On FRQs, explain why: 'nutrients are stored in biomass, so soils are thin.'
guide.cramSheet:
**Interactions:** predation · competition → resource partitioning · mutualism · commensalism · parasitism

**Biomes:** T + precip → plants · rainforest poor soil · tundra permafrost · desert < 25 cm

**C:** rock/ocean long-term · photosynthesis/respiration fast · fossil fuels → atmosphere

**N:** fixation → nitrification → assimilation → ammonification → denitrification

**P:** no gas · weathering · limiting in fresh water

**Productivity:** NPP = GPP − R · light bottle = NPP · dark bottle = R

**10% rule:** ÷10 per level · rest lost as heat

vocab.definition: Different species using the same resource in different ways, times, or places, reducing competition.
A large region defined by its climate and dominant vegetation.
Conversion of atmospheric N₂ into ammonia (NH₃) or ammonium (NH₄⁺) by bacteria or lightning.
Bacterial conversion of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate.
Conversion of nitrate back to N₂ gas by bacteria in low-oxygen conditions.
The nutrient in shortest supply relative to need, which controls growth.
Total rate at which producers capture energy by photosynthesis.
GPP minus energy used by producers in respiration; energy available to consumers.
A feeding position in a food chain (producer, primary consumer, etc.).
About 10% of energy at one trophic level is passed to the next.
Release of water vapor from plant leaves.
A place where a substance is stored in a biogeochemical cycle.

practice.stem: Which process converts atmospheric N₂ into a form that plants can absorb?

choices.text: Denitrification
Assimilation
Ammonification
Nitrogen fixation

practice.explanation: Fixation by bacteria (or lightning) converts N₂ into ammonia/ammonium.

distractors.A: Does the reverse: returns N₂ to the air.
distractors.C: Converts organic waste to ammonium, not N₂.

practice.stem: Phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient in freshwater lakes primarily because

choices.text: most phosphorus is stored in the atmosphere
it is rapidly removed from water by denitrifying bacteria
it has no significant gaseous phase and is released slowly from rock by weathering
plants cannot absorb phosphorus from water

practice.explanation: With no atmospheric reservoir, phosphorus enters ecosystems slowly through weathering, keeping supplies low.

practice.stem: A biome has permanently frozen subsoil, a growing season of about two months, and vegetation of mosses, lichens, and low shrubs. It is

choices.text: boreal forest
tundra
temperate grassland
cold desert

practice.explanation: Permafrost and a very short growing season define tundra.

distractors.A: Boreal forest supports conifers and lacks continuous permafrost near the surface in most areas.

practice.stimulus: Two bat species eat moths in the same forest. One forages just above the canopy at dusk; the other hunts close to the forest floor after midnight.
practice.stem: This pattern is best described as

choices.text: resource partitioning
mutualism
commensalism
competitive exclusion

practice.explanation: The species divide the prey resource by location and time, reducing direct competition.

distractors.D: Exclusion would mean one species eliminates the other.

practice.stem: A grassland has a gross primary productivity of 2,400 g C/m²/yr, and its plants use 1,500 g C/m²/yr in cellular respiration. What is its net primary productivity?

choices.text: 1,500 g C/m²/yr
900 g C/m²/yr
3,900 g C/m²/yr
0.63 g C/m²/yr

practice.stem: Producers in a lake capture 25,000 kcal/m²/yr. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to secondary consumers?

choices.text: 2,500 kcal/m²/yr
250 kcal/m²/yr
25 kcal/m²/yr
2.5 kcal/m²/yr

practice.stem: Which statement best explains why burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO₂ over time?

choices.text: It decreases the rate of photosynthesis worldwide.
It converts atmospheric oxygen directly into carbon dioxide without using any carbon.
It moves carbon from a long-term reservoir into the atmosphere faster than natural processes return it to long-term storage.
It releases carbon that was originally stored in the stratosphere.

practice.explanation: Fossil carbon accumulated over millions of years is released in decades; sinks (oceans, photosynthesis) cannot absorb it all.

distractors.D: Fossil fuel carbon comes from ancient organisms in sedimentary rock.

practice.stem: Estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth primarily because

choices.text: their constant salinity allows a few species to dominate
they receive no sediment, so the water is clear
they are deep enough to avoid temperature changes
rivers and tides continually deliver nutrients to shallow, sunlit water

practice.explanation: Nutrient-rich river water mixes with tidal water in shallow areas where light reaches producers.

practice.stem: Farmers notice that heavily waterlogged fields lose more applied nitrate fertilizer than well-drained fields, even with no runoff. Which process most likely explains this?

choices.text: Denitrification, because anaerobic bacteria in saturated soils convert nitrate to N₂ gas
Nitrogen fixation, because waterlogged soils hold more N₂
Nitrification, because waterlogged soils have more oxygen
Assimilation, because crops absorb more nitrate in wet soil

practice.explanation: Saturated soils lack oxygen, favoring denitrifying bacteria that release N₂ (and N₂O) to the air.

distractors.C: Nitrification requires oxygen; waterlogged soils have less.

practice.stimulus: Lake water starts with 8.0 mg/L dissolved oxygen. After 24 hours, a clear (light) bottle has 9.5 mg/L and an opaque (dark) bottle has 6.8 mg/L.
practice.stem: What is the gross primary productivity, in mg O₂/L/day?

practice.stimulus: In a kelp forest food web, sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. Many fish species shelter in kelp.
practice.stem: If sea otters were removed, which sequence is most likely?

choices.text: Urchins increase, kelp declines, fish that depend on kelp habitat decline
Urchins decrease, kelp increases, fish increase
Urchins increase, kelp increases, fish increase
No change, because otters are a small part of the food web

practice.explanation: Removing a top predator causes a trophic cascade: released herbivores overgraze producers, removing habitat for other species.

practice.stem: Large-scale clearing of a tropical rainforest for pasture is most likely to cause which change in the local water cycle?

choices.text: More transpiration and more local rainfall
No change, because rainfall comes only from the ocean
More groundwater recharge because soil is exposed
Less transpiration, less local rainfall, and more surface runoff and erosion

practice.explanation: Trees return much of the region's rainfall through transpiration. Without them, less water recycles to the air and more runs off compacted, exposed soil.

practice.stimulus: A climatograph shows monthly mean temperatures between 24 °C and 29 °C all year. Total annual precipitation is about 90 cm, almost all of it falling in six consecutive months; the other six months receive nearly none.
practice.stem: Which biome best matches this climatograph?

choices.text: Tropical rainforest
Hot desert
Savanna
Temperate deciduous forest

practice.explanation: Warm year-round with a long dry season and moderate total rainfall fits savanna.

distractors.A: Rainforest is wet all year and receives far more than 90 cm.

practice.stem: Which explanation best accounts for why a hectare of cropland can feed more people if they eat grain than if they eat grain-fed beef?

choices.text: Cattle convert most of the energy in grain to heat during metabolism, so eating one trophic level lower makes about ten times more energy available.
Grain contains more protein than beef.
Cattle recycle energy back into the soil.
Beef has fewer calories per kilogram than grain.

practice.explanation: Each trophic transfer loses roughly 90% of energy, mostly as metabolic heat.

practice.prompt:
Students investigate how primary productivity changes with depth in a lake. At each depth they fill a clear bottle and an opaque bottle with lake water, measure initial dissolved oxygen (DO), suspend the bottles at the depth where the water was collected, and measure DO again after 24 hours.

| Depth (m) | Initial DO (mg/L) | Clear bottle DO (mg/L) | Opaque bottle DO (mg/L) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.0 | 10.4 | 7.1 |
| 5 | 8.0 | 8.6 | 7.2 |
| 10 | 8.0 | 7.5 | 7.3 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable in this investigation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify one variable that should be held constant across depths.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Calculate the gross primary productivity at 1 m. Show your work.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why the clear bottle at 10 m ended with less oxygen than it started with.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Fertilizer runoff enters the lake. Explain how this would likely change productivity at 1 m in the short term.

parts.label: h
parts.prompt: Describe one human activity that increases turbidity in lakes, and propose one practice that would reduce it.

rubric.description: Change in dissolved oxygen / primary productivity.
E.g., bottle size, incubation time (24 h), time of day the bottles are set, same lake location.
Testable and directional, e.g., 'If depth increases, then GPP will decrease because less light reaches producers.'
Too little light reaches 10 m for photosynthesis to exceed respiration, so organisms consumed more O₂ than producers released.
Added nitrogen and phosphorus relieve nutrient limitation, so algae grow faster and productivity increases.
E.g., construction, clearcutting, or tilling near the shore increases sediment runoff.
E.g., planting vegetated riparian buffer strips, silt fences, no-till farming, or reforestation to hold soil in place.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Depth of the water.

(b) The change in dissolved oxygen, used to calculate primary productivity.

(c) The length of time the bottles are left in the lake (24 hours).

(d) If depth increases, then gross primary productivity will decrease, because less sunlight reaches the producers.

(e) NPP = 10.4 − 8.0 = 2.4 mg O₂/L/day. Respiration = 8.0 − 7.1 = 0.9 mg O₂/L/day. GPP = 2.4 + 0.9 = 3.3 mg O₂/L/day.

(f) At 10 m so little light penetrates that photosynthesis produces less oxygen than all organisms in the bottle consume by respiration, so DO falls.

(g) Fertilizer adds nitrogen and phosphorus, which are limiting nutrients. Algae near the surface would grow faster, increasing productivity at 1 m.

(h) Clearing land for construction near the lake exposes soil that washes in as sediment. Planting a vegetated buffer strip along the shoreline would trap sediment before it reaches the water.
